idiom: bite off more than one can chew
meaning: to take on a task or responsibility that is too big to manage
literal_translation: взяться за слишком большую задачу или обязанность, которую невозможно выполнить
example: The student bit off more than she could chew when she promised to revise the whole thesis in one week.
origin: A figurative image from eating: a mouthful that is too large cannot be chewed; the expression has been recorded in English since the 19th century

wrong_meanings.meaning: to eat a very large meal at a family dinner
wrong_meanings.why_wrong: The idiom is figurative and has nothing to do with food; it describes overcommitting to a task

wrong_meanings.meaning: to chew gum noisily during a lecture
wrong_meanings.why_wrong: The idiom does not describe chewing habits; it refers to taking on more than one can manage

wrong_meanings.meaning: to bite a piece of wood in a carpentry workshop
wrong_meanings.why_wrong: This takes the words literally; the idiom refers to a mistaken ambition, not to physical action

explanation: 'Bite off more than one can chew' means to agree to do more work or take on more responsibility than one can realistically handle. It is often used in discussions of academic and professional planning, when a person has overestimated their capacity.
